caption:
A false positive is not a shrug. It is a cost.

Every alarm that turns out to be nothing spends something real: a patrol diverted, a shift pulled off another task, an adviser's attention for the next ten alerts. Cry wolf three times on a quiet pass and the fourth alert — the real one — gets a slower read. That is the actual price of a bad detection, not embarrassment, lost response capacity.

This is why a serious system does not output yes or no. It outputs confirmed, assessed, or unknown, with the reasoning attached. An anomaly against baseline is a lead, not a verdict. Corroboration — a second pass, a different sensor type, a pattern that holds over time — is what moves it from lead to call. Skipping that step is cheaper to build and more expensive to trust.

The discipline is not technical. It is restraint: stating what is known, flagging what is not, and never letting urgency round an unknown up to a confirmed.

This is why the output is graded — confirmed, assessed, unknown — not a binary alarm. Restraint is the discipline, not a limitation.

card.headline: A false alarm still costs something
card.sub: Every unconfirmed alert spends response capacity and trust. Grading confidence is how that cost gets managed, not avoided.

rationale: Covers the false-positive-cost angle from the brief with fresh framing (operational trust cost, not the already-used hotspot/cause wording), teaching a concrete analytic concept with no product pitch.
